title: How does a zipper work?

sections.html:
A zipper closes when its slider guides two rows of teeth together. Pull it the other way and the slider separates them.

The teeth, also called elements, sit on two fabric strips. YKK’s explanation of zipper construction shows how those pieces work together.
sections.title: A little machine hiding on your pencil case

sections.html:
Look at a zip on a bag or jacket. These are its three main parts.

The parts to look for on a zipper
PartWhere to lookWhat it does
Teeth, or elementsThe rows beside the openingFit together to close the gap
SliderThe small body behind the tab you pullGuides the teeth together or apart
TapeThe fabric strip on each sideCarries the row of teeth

The pull tab is your handle, not the whole slider. Both appear in YKK’s zipper manual (page 1).
sections.title: Find these three parts

sections.html:
Inside the slider, a Y-shaped passage guides two rows into one joined chain. The separate rows enter the wide end; their teeth fit together and leave through the narrow end.

Opening reverses the trip. The slider guides the movement; the teeth hold the zip together.
sections.title: Inside the slider is a tiny Y-shaped passage

sections.html:
In Gideon Sundback’s 1917 fastener patent, each tooth has a hollow on one side and a raised bump on the other. A bump fits into a neighbouring hollow.

The shape lets the teeth hold together, while the sliding guide connects or separates their rows.
sections.title: The clever bit is in the shape

sections.html:
Holding the teeth together and keeping the slider still are different jobs. Some sliders have a small locking pin that catches on the teeth. Moving the pull tab releases it.

Details vary between mechanisms; YKK shows both locking designs.
sections.title: Some zips have a hidden brake, too

sections.html:
If you have a freely moving bag zip, slowly close a short section. Watch beside the slider; stop if fabric catches.

Which part moves along the opening?

The slider moves. The teeth stay attached to their fabric strips, joining as the slider passes.

Compare this with the fastener inspired by a burr, then meet the ball inside a ballpoint pen. Small objects can hide surprisingly clever mechanisms.
